::: {.why}
The overlap counts you plotted last night mean your hundred thousand training rows contain far fewer independent observations, and every standard error in the phase depends on knowing how many.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Compute average uniqueness per observation and derive the effective sample size of your training set.
- Say what an inflated effective sample size does to a model comparison, and in which direction.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>65 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Implement uniqueness in qlib/ml/labels.py: for each observation, the average over its label window of the reciprocal of the number of concurrent labels. Then report the effective sample size as the sum of uniqueness across the training set, against the raw row count. The ratio is often four or five to one.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Show what it changes: recompute the standard error of your out-of-sample R-squared using the effective sample size rather than the row count, and note how many model comparisons that reclassifies from significant to indistinguishable. This is the same correction as clustering standard errors, applied to a machine learning workflow that usually does not do it at all.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Note the second use: bagging with a sample size set by uniqueness rather than by the row count, which is where tomorrow starts.
:::
:::
